en: The First Hymn, titled *Bhaktivilāsa*: Om!
We bow to that devotee who possesses true devotion, for whom the splendor of Śiva manifests in this very way, even without meditating or chanting according to prescribed rules. (UtSst 1.1)
Although my soul is young, having drunk the nectar of devotion to you, it has become grey, as if with hoary hairs, from the dust and passion of worldly life. (UtSst 1.2)
For those inhabitants of your city who possess devotion and have attained that perfection,
their movement even upon the path of the world may occur through that very same manifestation.
O Lord, since you are manifest as everything within the entire universe, what place is not a field for those possessed of devotion? For them, what mantra would not be accomplished?
O Lord, those who are always Your second [companions] are victorious— though they are themselves without a second, they are intoxicated by the excellent nectar-wine of the essence of devotion.
O Lord, those who are drenched in the essence of the bliss of intense devotion— those alone know Your true nature, You who are an ocean of infinite bliss.
"O Lord of the Self, you alone are the self of all, and all is within the self;
thus, knowing that devotion to you is established by its very nature, a person shall conquer [all]. (UtSst 1.7)
O Lord, when the objects of knowledge have ceased, by what means are You not seen standing alone?
Yet, even amidst the agitation of the known and the knower, You are easily perceived by Your devotees.
Just as Queen Anantānandasarasī is your most beloved and remains inseparable from you, so may my singular devotion to you likewise be.
O Lord, for those possessed of devotion, every state of yours is a cause for attainment;
this path of consciousness exists in three ways, through joy, suffering, and delusion.
O Lord, that supreme state of awakening which arises from tasting the nectar of devotion to you is,
for me, like the sourness of wine.
Those in whom the great science of devotion to you has reached the stage of mastery are knowers of reality, even if they possess both knowledge and ignorance. (UtSst 1.12)

May this creeper of speech, which has its root in you and flourishes through gradual expansion, be sprinkled with the nectar of devotion to you and bear for me fruits rich in that very essence. (UtS 1.13)
"One should worship having become Śiva" is said to mean "having become a devotee";
for you alone are the essence of the body, purified as non-dual by devotees. (UtS 1.14)
What arguments are not available for the establishment of the non-duality of existence for devotees?
And what veils are not present for the lowly to prevent that realization? (UtS 1.15)
"O Lord, it is a deception to say that you are found somewhere by yoga only at some time;
otherwise, how could you manifest in all spheres for those possessed of devotion? (UtS 1.16)
There is this great distinction, untouched by [the need for] withdrawal and the other [limbs of yoga]:
that those who possess devotion remain concentrated even during the state of emergence from meditation, unlike the practitioners of yoga. (UtS 1.17)
Neither yoga, nor austerity, nor any ritual sequence is prescribed here;
in this illusion-free path of Śiva, singular devotion alone is praised.
For me, whose obscurations have been destroyed by the splendor of devotion shining forth from all sides and who perceive all phenomena directly, may even thoughts perish.
Aha! For those devoted ones, there is a certain indescribable savoring of all objects of experience, even while the single word "Śiva" constantly rests upon the tip of their tongue. (UtS 1.20)

In the ocean of the nectar of devotion—which is cool, pure, sweet, and with its waves stilled—who indeed can be counted among those who are well-established in the tasting of this extraordinary aesthetic flavor? (UtSst 1.21)
O Blessed One, why would those like us not relish the great medicine of devotion to you, which possesses such a flavor that liberation itself is its immediate essence? (UtS 1.22)
O Lord, those very attainments are considered supreme by the virtuous which nourish the confidence of enjoying the essence of devotion to you. (UtSst 1.23)
Those who have been touched in some way by the nectar-showers of devotion to you are not defiled by this mire of passion and the like, even though they have fallen into it. (UtS 1.24)

The description of the fruits pertains specifically to the limbs beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with liberation, just as certain parts of a creeper are described when its devotion to existence has reached maturity. (UtSst 1.25)
O Lord, this mind is by nature a wondrous seed of suffering;
yet when sprinkled with the essence of devotion to you, it bears the great fruit of supreme bliss.
The second hymn, titled "The Cultivation of the Universal Self":

Homage to You, whose nature consists of pure consciousness, who possess many forms—the essence of Agni, Soma, Ravi, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, and the very self of all that is moving and unmoving. (UtSst 2.1)
Homage to the Great Fire, whose pure radiance is enhanced by the application of the great ash of all fuel, and who is the sole oblation for the entire universe.
Salutations be to You, the fire of Śiva, who is dense with supreme nectar and cool, yet who is like a venomous serpent to the universal conflagration. UtSst_2.3 //
Salutations to Mahādeva, to Rudra, to Śaṅkara, to Śiva,
and also to Maheśvara— to that certain one whose form is the mantra.

Homage to the auspicious fire of Śiva, which, though its unevenness is intensified by the sprinkling of the fat dripping from the three worlds as they are cut down and dried up, is nonetheless a source of blessing.
Salutations to that certain god Śambhu, for whom the very application of all defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Homage to the one who is not in contradiction with the Vedas and Āgamas, who establishes the Vedas and Āgamas, who is the true essence of the Vedas and Āgamas, the secret one, the Lord.
Homage to Śambhu, who is the sole cause of saṃsāra, yet the sole adversary of saṃsāra; who has the form of saṃsāra, yet is himself beyond saṃsāra.
Homage to the one who is root, middle, and tip; whose form consists of root, middle, and tip;
whose root, middle, and tip are extinguished; the full Śambhu.
Homage to you, the auspicious one, so difficult to encounter, for even a single utterance of whose name is the ripening of the accumulation of well-performed deeds.
Homage to you, the solitary Lord who wears a skull, who consists of pure consciousness, and who eternally sports with hosts of spirits in the form of all that moves and is immobile.
Homage to the master of illusion, the pure one, the secret one, whose nature is manifest;
to the subtle one, whose form is the universe, the manifold one, the source of bliss.
Homage to you, the one possessed of all powers, who performs the wondrous sport of the destruction of the world, brought to completion by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.
Homage to you, O ocean whose depths are unfathomable, by whom those various prosperities were obtained while wandering along the very shores.
Homage to the beautiful Śambhu-lotus, which dwells amidst the thick mud of the world composed of illusion, yet remains unstained.
Homage to you, who are auspicious, pure, a treasury, the very essence of ornament,
beloved, the ultimate reality, and the most excellent of all.
Homage to that certain Śambhu, who is eternally bound yet eternally liberated, who is devoid of both bondage and liberation. (UtSst 2.17)
In these three worlds, whose sole essence is mockery, homage be to you alone, the peerless one who dwells in eternal bliss. (UtS 2.18)
Homage to you, Śarva, whose essence is the conduct of the right-hand path, who desires the conduct of the left-hand path, who is the conduct of all, yet who is beyond all conduct.
In whatever way and whoever he may be who is worthy of worship, wherever he may be and however he is honored— be he this one or that one, whichever deity he may be— homage be to you!
Homage to you, the bestower of boons, who possesses expansive beauty, who is served by those seeking liberation, and who removes all suffering.
Homage to you, the Lord who is the eternal festival, for whom the entire three worlds are perpetually filled with the essence of uninterrupted bliss.
And because he enjoys you alone through the enjoyments that are primarily experienced as bliss,
homage to you, the host of Śaktis, for that formidable [deity].
Salutations to that certain Being whom even the sages cannot comprehend, yet whom those whose actions are bound by devotion embrace.
Homage be to you, the treasury of supreme nectar, the mass of supreme nectar,
who has reached the further shore of all perfections.
I bow to your form, which consists of the great mantra, pure and cool,
blessed with unprecedented joy, and overflowing with the essence of supreme nectar.
I bow to Your teaching, O Lord, wherein— because it is filled with the nectar of absolute freedom— there is no diversity whatsoever on the great canvas of the manifestation of unity.
We praise the path of Maheśvara, which is the thunderbolt that destroys all doubts, the fire of time for all misfortune, and the end of all inauspiciousness.
Victory to you, O God! Homage, homage be unto you! This entire universe is dependent upon you;
you are the Supreme Lord of the worlds, the one supreme being. I have come to you for refuge.

The third hymn, titled *Praṇayaprasāda* (Grace through Affection): Homage to the wondrous Śambhu, the third [state], who transcends that twofold course of existence consisting of being and non-being. (UtSst 3.1)

In these three worlds, which are not independent due to the presence of Asuras, Rishis, and other beings, those who are dependent upon you alone—the Independent One—are themselves truly independent. (UtS 3.2)
Those for whom the recollection of your body, which is inlaid with the entirety of the universe, is the sole remedy for the diseases of existence, are seated in happiness. (UtS 3.3)
He whose white parasol is the moon, filled with its own radiance,
and whose fly-whisk is the stream of the celestial river— he alone is the Supreme Lord.
O Lord, bestow upon me some indescribable vision— one that is luminous, cool, singular, and pure like a digit of the moon, and which flows with the stream of nectar.
O Blessed One, how is it that these droplets of consciousness fallen from the ocean of your consciousness-bliss are so beautiful with the taste of nectar? (UtSst 3.6)
O Lord, O Master, those whose hearts are not immersed in the essence of passion for you are truly heartless; such as these are merely a fit object for contempt.
He with whom you, the Lord, have achieved a union of hearts,
is the sole supreme recipient of all sovereign splendors.
Then, the flood of the nectar of your meditation equally washes away all joys and sorrows, just as water flows down through ever-deepening hollows on the earth.
O Lord, how could those not be filled with an abundance of happiness, for whom there is nowhere any separation from You, who are greater than their own selves? (UtS 3.10)
I roar indeed, I dance; my heart's desires are fulfilled! For you, who are exceedingly pleasing, have been made my lord. (UtS 3.11)

Where there is no other object of knowledge, no action, and no other yoga apart from consciousness itself; what could that knowledge be? Rather, it is the singular, full universal consciousness that unfolds.
From the hands of those from whose speech the sound of "Śiva" ever resounds, infinite and invincible sufferings have suddenly fled away. (UtS 3.13)
There is another Supreme Person distinguished by being the remnant of you;
but you alone are the Great Person, the refuge of all persons without exception.
Victorious are those servants of yours, O Lord of the worlds, who are worthy of the world's veneration;
for them, this very ocean of saṃsāra is but a great pleasure-lake for their play.
Let other forms of wretchedness experienced by those dwelling in this world be set aside for a moment;
you yourself, O Lord, are ashamed by this very fact: "May you manifest yourself. (UtS 3.16)
"There is nothing beyond me; moreover, I am the reciter because of that unity.
In reality, this is what you sometimes indicate as 'recitation' by means of the rosary. (UtSst 3.17)
O Lord, that which is supreme is necessarily non-existent, yet it is beyond even that which exists;
and since You are other than both the non-existent and the existent, You are composed of both existence and non-existence.
Though you possess a pure radiance exceeding the rays of a thousand suns,
and though you pervade all worlds, you are not seen.
In this inert world, you are indeed of the nature of consciousness; even amidst the knowable, you are the knower.
Since you are all-pervading even within the limited, you are therefore the supreme among all.
Enough with other lamentations; O Lord, I shall cry out only this much before you: "O Protector, though I know this, I am utterly bewildered."
The Fourth Hymn, titled *Surāsodbalā*.

O mind, even though you are fickle, you are nevertheless to be praised because you take refuge in the beloved of Ambikā, the teacher of the three worlds, who is the refuge even of those who seek refuge.
Having ascended the various steps of the deities and reached the feet of Śiva, even though I have taken refuge on this lower ground, I still do not abandon my wonder— how strange!
Reveal your own path and completely shroud the activities of all the worlds,
O Blessed One, so that I may instantly become your ever-risen servant.
O Śiva, Śiva, Śambhu, Śaṅkara, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, quickly bestow your compassion!
For indeed, for one devoted to the remembrance of your pair of lotus feet, prosperity is not far off.
O Lord, those who, reclining upon the seat of Your lotus feet, create the world according to their own pleasure,
laugh at Viriñci, who is defiled by the impurity of office and is not master of himself.
Nothing whatsoever capable of appearing exists apart from your luminous body;
therefore, O Blessed One, you are eternally attained, yet, O Lord, you remain far removed even from primordial nature (prakṛti).
Some have approached the nectar of your lotus feet with a disposition steeped in dualism; yet others taste it immediately as it appears, undecaying in form and devoid of duality.

O Lord, that which once shone for me like lightning at dawn, now smeared with nectar—if that were to become truly stable, then you would be worshipped according to the rite; what more could be said? (UtSst 4.8)
"Everything else is inferior; there is no other thing whatsoever, whether real or unreal. Having resolved this through great wisdom, be just as you are, clearly manifest to me.
O Blessed One, it was by Your own will that I was made to set foot upon Your own path by You, the Lord;
how then can I act like an ordinary person? I do not understand anything worthy of Your feet.
O Lord, some supreme state of blessedness expands within their hearts,
by which even they have long been made fortunate, like *cātaka* birds at the sound of the clouds of your speech.
Through some playful sport of yours, this passion of those devoted to you has reached full maturity;
for even conversation and remembrance regarding the land of separation yield the festival of union. (UtSst 4.12)
This word "Śaṅkara," which has been nourished by the sprinkling of various aesthetic flavors and uttered hundreds of times, enters even the minds of animals; it possesses ever-new purposes.
Victorious are those in whose faces the sound of "Śiva" constantly revolves, which,
like the moon spread forth from the ocean of nectar, flows out as the most delicious ambrosia.
This world appears as if brought to an end, for the dense impurity of the mind has dissolved;
yet, not even an atom of the striking against the bolts and door-panels of the city of existence has ceased.
O Lord, my mind is yearning to behold the interior of your lotus-face, which is perpetually in bloom; therefore, perform some slight act by which you might remain facing me.
What other happiness is there in this world than the realization that one is non-different from you? And what other prosperity is there?
Therefore, why does the mind of your servant here stray onto a wrong path, having abandoned that [realization]?
I would indeed not be a fit vessel for even a moment’s service to you here, were I not to constantly and with devotion savor the intoxicating nectar of the flavor of non-duality with you. (UtS 4.18)
"Truly, these people do not see the reality of your form, being defiled by the vision of duality;
yet, you who know all and are compassionate toward those who depend on you—why do you not hear this cry of mine?"
O Lord, do you perhaps recall even once that sensual pleasure which was desired by me?
Nevertheless, I have requested only this: grant me fully that nectar of constantly beholding your form, which is my true desire.
"O Maheśa, by Your will, at the very moment I have set foot upon Your auspicious path, hundreds of blessings have arisen for me; what else, O Lord, could I possibly seek from You? (UtSst 4.21)
Wherein that Sun goes to his setting along with the Moon and all the other luminaries—
victorious is that Śivarātri, whose form is radiant with the spreading effulgence of its own light.
O Lord of the Immortals, I consider even the sovereignty over the three worlds that I have acquired to be sapless, for it is devoid of the nectar-like essence of touching your feet. (UtS 4.23)
Alas, Lord! This firm bond of the self, consisting of the non-recognition of You, was fashioned by You alone;
for even as it manifests before me, it does not slacken even in the slightest, despite Your presence.
O Lord of the Immortals, though you are constantly being worshipped by the great ones, you remain as the singular form of the worshipper;
appearing both externally and internally here, you eternally manifest within the very body of the beholder.
The Fifth Hymn, titled "The Instruction on One's Own Strength":
O Lord, by means of the *galepādika* [the "neck-tether"], cause me— who am attached solely to the enjoyment of contact with the lotus of Your feet— to enter Your own abode.
When shall I have my hair colored by the mass of pollen from the lotus-feet of your honor,
and perform a dance commenced with boundless impetuosity?
O Blessed One, having you as my sole protector, I always request only this:
may I dwell within you in silence, and never again be a wise man [in the worldly sense].
"O Treasure of Nectar, O Lord! O Pure One, O Three-Eyed One!
O Taste, O Odd-Eyed One!"—thus crying out, I would dance.
With eyes closed from the touch of your lotus feet,
may I yawn, reeling from the intoxication of the wine of devotion to you.
O Lord, may I dwell as a mountain of mind upon some spot on earth where my state of being—
consisting of nothing but your incessant talk— may find its great aesthetic flavor.
In that city where you, accompanied by the Goddess, stood in many forms from the palace to the gate-tower, there I shall become a resident.
May the rays of the sun that is your being shine forth, O Blessed One,
so that this lotus of my heart may blossom for your worship.
Be gracious, O Blessed One; may my mind, which has fallen forever at your feet, savor that [state] and as it were dissolve and vanish away. (UtSst 5.9)
Whether out of great joy or even out of sorrow, whether from a wall or even from a pillar,
manifest yourself to me, O Lord, from whatever external or internal state you may be!
May that extremely cooling nectar of the touch of your lotus feet flow for me always, both externally and internally. (UtS 5.11)
May there always be for me this indescribable enjoyment, which consists of immersion in the nectar-essence of the touch of your feet— an experience that transcends all worldly pleasures.
"O Blessed One, please accept from me these passions and so forth that have been offered;
having taken them and transformed them into nectar, partake of them together with your devotees. (UtSst 5.13)
O Lord, you who are eternally satisfied by consuming the entirety of the worlds, please grant your servants the moment of your gracious glance as a seat of happiness.

With eyes closed in the savoring of the wonder of internal devotion, even blades of grass would become objects of worship for me as I offer them with the thought, "Salutation to Śiva, who is myself. (UtS 5.15)
May I, having attained the realization of existence as non-existence, behold the world as consisting of the radiance of my own self, never separated from the full enjoyment of the flavor of devotion.
O Protector, since there exists nothing else that you could desire, it is fitting that you, who are without a second, possess complete perfection.
May I attain that state where laughter and dance occur, where passion, hatred, and the like are consumed, and where the nectar-essence of devotion is drunk. (UtSst 5.18)
May that fragrance of the flower of contemplation on the touch of unprecedented delight attain firmness in my mind, so that the scent of evil tendencies may not fade away. (UtSst 5.19)
Where indeed is passion among lust and the like, and where is the state of being impassioned toward the lotus-feet of Hara?
O immortal one, awaken my heart, which thus relishes such contradiction, to what is beneficial.
Even while wandering through the stages of yoga, though remaining withdrawn from sense objects,
may my heart be made tremulous with the intoxication of the wine of meditation upon you.
May the flavor of devotion always be my forerunner in speech, mind, and thought, as well as in all bodily movements performed by the instruments [of the senses]. (UtSst 5.22)
O Lord, while this name of yours, "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva," is being recited without end, may I experience some indescribable, unsurpassed great flavor within existence. (UtSst 5.23)

May I wander as your honored servant in this universe whose essence is the throbbing infinite consciousness, wherein all paths of insentient matter have been swallowed up, and which is filled with countless other clusters of pure spirit.

"Nothing whatsoever is required for that which is established as eternal and clearly manifest within one's own body"—may this conviction become firmly rooted in me, who am purified by the dust of your lotus feet. (UtSst 5.25)
O Lord, may that something which occasionally flashes forth in the minds of those who touch the soles of your feet—
that in which this entire universe dissolves like a world of nectar— be forever directed toward me.

O Īśāna, may this sixth hymn, titled *Adhvavisphuraṇa*, become for even a mere moment the object of the vision of me who am separated from you and who am perpetually tormented by intense suffering. (UtSst 6.1)
In this saṃsāra, whose essence is separation, may I never be separated from you, my beloved lord, even if I am separated from the entire world.
"Whatever I go toward with body, speech, and mind, all that is you alone"—may this ultimate truth also be ever perfectly fulfilled for me. (UtSst 6.3)
Just as you are non-conceptual and filled with great bliss,
so too may my speech, which offers praise to you, be truly worthy of you.
Perceiving every state of being as consisting of existence through the penetration of that very existence,
may I wander free from longing and filled with supreme joy.
O Blessed One, I would be satisfied with seeing the entire world as full [of you]; therefore, you do not become weary.
May all phenomena shine within me eternally as they proceed toward progressive purification, dissolving right into you, like fragments of clouds into the sky.
May some indescribable jewel of yours shine forth continuously from the midst of existence for me— a jewel whose spreading radiance destroys the endless succession of darkness.
Upon which stage do you not dwell? What could that be which is not your body, so that through effortless exertion I might obtain you everywhere?
O Lord, when this has been attained, let the enjoyment of embracing your limbs happen according to my own will; what then remains for me that has not been conquered?
Manifest yourself! We do not cause you distress with other prayers, O Lord; we, yearning, seek only you.

O Lord Ānandasarasvatī, may my mind, having attained a state of equanimity with You, abandon through this single act this great calamity rooted in duality, by means of this seventh hymn named *Vidhuravijaya*.

O Lord, let the axe of the realization of oneness with You fall within me— upon that deep-rooted foundation of the shackles of passion, hatred, and the like, which say, "This is mine, but this is not."
May the series of stains of conceptual construction dissolve; may unimpeded freedom shine forth in my heart; O Blessed One, may my mind-made form be drenched in the essence of bliss.
May the Mother, who is the contemplation of devotion to You, nourish me with those various essences that have been churned from the egg of existence consisting of passion and the like,
so that I may become a bird whose wings are fully grown.

May this mind of mine attain the skill of tasting the essence of the nectar-juice of the meditation upon your feet, until the latent tendencies of attachment to the poison of sense objects are entirely exhausted.
By the power of contact with the rays of the sun of devotion to you,
may this jewel of my mind cast far away the sparks of the fire of passion and other afflictions that torment it.
In that state, I would constantly extol you most loudly,
wherein even Hari, Haryaśva, and Viriñca wait outside.
Under the influence of the rapture born of devotion, may I perceive with all my senses the entire world as consisting of Śiva, and all actions as consisting of worship. (UtSst 7.8)
Having given birth to children such as the *aṇimā* powers from the family-women who are your devotees— women held within my own mind—
may they strengthen the firmly rooted conviction that "these are mine."
The eighth hymn, titled "Supernatural Empowerment":
When will that fragment of the Lord’s grace residing within me and this devotion which has come to me like a lover— these two, joined together— attain full maturity in such a body?
May some indescribable essence of satisfaction, born from the constant relishing of your sovereignty, arise within me;
may this alone be my supreme state at all times here, while the greatness of knowledge, yoga, and so forth remain far behind.
O Blessed One, let my intense thirst for sense-objects remain as it is, like that of worldly people;
only this I ask: may I behold these objects as being your very body, free from all conceptual constructions.
Thus, having entered into the body, the ground, the mind, the path of the vital breath,
and the paths of consciousness, may you become manifest to me as my very own self.
O Lord, let these functions of my senses, though they may surge forth, fall back into their respective stations;
for even for a moment, let there never be the audacity of a slight loss of the flavor of non-difference from You.
Meditating, by virtue of being possessed by [the deity], upon a body that is light, smooth, white, transparent, and cool,
may I transcend those worldly activities pertaining to the entire range of objects.
May my own body, which is of the nature of existence, blossom; may all worlds attain the state of being my very limbs;
and may all this flickering of duality become ineffable even upon the path of memory.
May there arise for me a flood of the nectar of beholding such a forest of yours,
so that it may fill the terrible cave of the non-manifestation of your non-duality.
Will I ever, by being sprinkled with even the slightest drop of the nectar of union with you,
become averse to all worldly pleasures— will I not indeed fall from both?
O Unborn One, may the lotus-stalk of devotion arise for me— this supreme swan who constantly wanders in the pond of Your lotus feet— from the very root, from the surface, and from within.
O Lord, may all things come within the range of my thought and the field of my vision;
may they shine forth supremely as the very essence of the nectar of the light of my perception and reflection.
O Supreme Lord, may I indeed be present for them even when those various hardships arise—
not only so that they are free from fear, but also so that they experience an even greater joy born from contact with Your body.
Since the entire universe is woven within you and is manifested by you alone externally, let that which is attended by this firm conviction now shine forth with utter clarity. (UtSst 8.13)

When will my mind, abandoning all else, become eager for the touch of you— the touch that is ever-ardent with the savoring of union moistened by the nine aesthetic sentiments? This is the ninth hymn, titled *Svātantryavijaya*.
"Devoted solely to you, with the mere worship of your feet as my great wealth, when shall I, filled with longing, behold you face to face? (UtSst 9.2)

When, under the sway of intense passion, my mind shall have become indifferent [to worldly things], and all the great bolts [of the city of existence] shall burst open with a *paṭapaṭ* sound—at that time, I shall come to you. (UtS 9.3)
O Lord, when shall I bring under my control all the deities, who are established in the heart that is the essence of self-awareness, through the power of my devotion to you?
O Lord, when will there be for me that great festival of the essence of bliss born of devotion,
wherein even my name shall be obtained as one who rejoices in the happiness of beholding You?
When shall I, having suddenly recognized my master— who is the Lord, fearless, noble, perfect, causeless, and whose very self is hidden— put him to shame?
O Lord, when shall I attain that certain belovedness of yours,
by which it would never be right for you to flee from me?
O Lord, when shall I be flooded by the taste of seeing and rejoicing in all sentient beings in reality as being of the nature of your worship? (UtS 9.8)
O All-pervading Lord, when will my longing for that devotion to you—devotion which is the supreme ground of knowledge and the highest state of yoga—be fulfilled? UtSst_9.9 //
When will I suddenly seize you firmly today, overcome with joy,
and manifest to all the supreme treasure that is your feet?
O Lord, when shall I become one whose nature consists of the light of purity spreading everywhere, such that no stain from the shadow of illusion remains for me?
O Blessed One, when shall I become a leader of the host of your devotees, having brought the entire mandala under my own control and being free from all worldly concern?
O Lord, you are the unprecedented foundation for those who possess worldly pride;
when shall I, filled with the essence of devotion to you, become one of great pride?
When shall I lie down, as it were, upon a pair of cool-limbed lotuses, firmly established in the embrace of the glory that is empty of all objective domains?
When shall I reach the further shore of this abundance of the enjoyment of your worship, which is enriched by the wine of devotion? When shall I become one who has accomplished his purpose?
When, with a cry faltering and agitated by tears of joy,
my face brightened by a smile, shall I attain the essence of the taste of touching you?
O Śambhu, when shall I cast aside this state, which is the common way of life for mere cattle,
and experience my own true nature as is fitting for one devoted to You?

When shall I be one who has attained the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, whose fear of all afflictions and calamities has vanished, and who is intent on the play of drinking the elixir of the flavor of devotion to You? (UtSst 9.18)
O Lord, when will that cry of mine ever issue from my speech, so that immediately upon its utterance, your form may manifest before me?
When shall I, my mind intent on the addiction of embracing your lotus feet with ever-deepening fervor, behold you— this reality that is yet not a thing— at no effort at all?

This tenth hymn, titled "The Indestructible and Uninterrupted," must certainly not be endured by you, O sole Lord of the world, since it is equal toward both the devotees of Maheśvara and other people. (UtS 10.1)
Those who always follow your feet with devotion enjoy various pleasures wherever they may go.
Where you, the Lord who is Time and the Ender, are present, whence can there be afflictions?
And where your own Fortune resides, what desire for other enjoyments could exist there?
Since you, the All-pervading Lord, can be attained even through a moment’s happiness,
therefore every moment of his life is filled with the bliss of you.
A drop of the essence of bliss from you has fallen as the moon upon the earth;
likewise, the sun has issued forth from you as a particle of light that effects destruction.
O Lord, we offer this oblation to this third eye of yours,
which is the sole emblem of some world-transcending majesty.
You have been seen by him alone who rejoices exceedingly at the sight of you;
or rather, you have been beheld by someone in whom some kind of joy has somehow arisen.
O Lord, those with whom you are pleased have truly gained your heart;
for having drawn them from your outer city, you have made them your inner ones.
Behold: apart from you, the entire universe has become equal in your vision;
yet you alone, O Lord with the uneven eyes, remain its sovereign.
Let it be; for without your power, even existence itself would not exist, since the talk of those who find fault with you cannot be sustained apart from you.
O Lord, if my mind were to abide in You— who are free from the false duality of external and internal obstacles— what else would be required?
O Blessed One, some wander while being extremely ill-established in the self;
O Blessed One, others wander while being extremely well-established in the self.
O Lord, even without drinking the nectar of devotion to you and without beholding you,
living beings attain perfection merely through your exemplary conduct.
O Lord, we are your servants, just as you sustain the three worlds;
in that same manner, we too are fully capable of being sustained by you.
O Soul of the World, though I have beheld You who consist of the nectar of supreme bliss, I am nonetheless intensely longing for the essence of Your touch.
O Lord, all the sufferings without exception that belong to those in cyclic existence become endurable when joined with your self, which is called "Fortitude."
O Lord, since you alone are omniscient, omnipotent, and composed of consciousness,
the manifestation of this world— which is in every respect non-existent— is nonetheless possible through you.
Animated by you, these qualities vibrate even though they are like clods of earth;
they dance like tufts of cotton wool tossed by the wind.
O Lord, if there were no self-conceit regarding qualities, then by what could the world's renown of its being of one essence with you be diminished? (UtS 10.19)
O Supreme Lord, even those most venerable ones who have met their end are worthy of worship, for they are purified by the touch of the fire of Your wrath.
O Lord, since that great luminous body remains clearly manifest everywhere, why then do I spread forth into darkness?
You alone, undivided, are my own immortal nature;
nevertheless, I am the sole abode of those subject to the laws of mortality.
He alone is truly empowered who possesses the name "Maheśvara" as an ornament of speech and bears the mark of prostration upon his head. (UtS 10.23)

O Blessed One, since you yourself effortlessly and spontaneously [know] both the existent and the non-existent by whatever means, why is it that my own accomplishment does not likewise come about? (UtS 10.24)
What happiness could Śivadāsa, whose very self is Śiva, not attain—he by whom I am gratified with the nectar-liquors even of the foremost gods? (UtS 10.25)
Residing in the space between the heart and the navel, you are the embodiment of bile for living beings;
as the great fire, you consume all that is stationary and moving.
The eleventh hymn, titled "The Trusting of Eager Longing":
This world, or rather, neither friends nor kinsmen, belong to me in any way;
since you, however, are all this, who else could there be for me? (UtS 11.1)
"O Lord, you are Maheśvara himself; you alone are the entire world"—even such a prayer that "the reality itself may attain perfection" is merely a prayer. (UtSst 11.2)
O Lord, for one who enjoys worldly existence, even sovereignty over the three worlds appears here like a blade of grass;
what fruit, then, could there be for such a person of virtuous deeds other than the remembrance of you? (UtSst_11.3)
Since there is nothing whatsoever in the worlds that exists apart from you, and since even the origin of all beings is your own manifestation,
no composition of praise can arise for you, even regarding your wondrous deeds.

O Lord, if I am permeated by You and remain constantly devoted to Your worship, meditating upon this without ceasing through my own natural inclination—even while dreaming—how could I not be exactly like that? (UtSst_11.5)
For those who have been touched even slightly by a fragment of the fragrance arising from the lotus-feet of Your Honor,
all the multitude of enjoyments sought after even by the immortals becomes like a foul stench.
O Śambhu, there is nothing else in your heart, nor anything else in your speech or in your action;
even toward one who exists in the ultimate sense, either grace or restraint must be exercised as a single, uniform purpose.

I am deluded, I am afflicted by suffering, I am afraid of the defects of old age and the like, I am devoid of power, and I have taken refuge in you; O Śambhu, therefore act swiftly so that, having abandoned the path of suffering, I may attain the most supreme station.
Having rested upon the region of your ear, my most insignificant lamentations attain a state of great value;
they bear the likeness of pearls, just as fragments of water falling into the interior of a bamboo stalk assume the nature of pearl gems.
O Lord, what indeed is not obtained even by those people who are devoted to your name for even a moment, even if it be out of hypocrisy?

O you who have the moon as your crest-jewel, act in such a way that I may attain the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and the other supernatural faculties, having overcome death according to my capacity.

O Śambhu, O Śarva, O you who have the moon as your crest-jewel, O Śiva, O three-eyed one, O bearer of the rosary, O glorious one marked by the fierce skull, O you whose weapon is the gleaming and terrible trident!
O ocean of compassion, O you whose nature is the fierce power that fashions the three worlds, O Śrīkaṇṭha, quickly destroy the burden of my inauspiciousness and bestow upon me supreme accomplishment.

Therefore, O Lord, could there be anything where the Blessed One does not exercise his creative power? And how could there be the destruction of that which possesses consciousness, since Śaṅkara is its creator?
Thus, though you—the Supreme Lord—possess an ever-unassailable great power, I alone suffer here in this saṃsāra, distressed by incessant afflictions.

Even if these—suffering, old age, and death, which are most arrogant in granting boons—were to remain for a moment, or even if the unstable objects of the senses such as sound were highly esteemed; nevertheless, longing for perpetual happiness, I desire for a long time that supreme life-force consisting of meditation upon Your lotus feet, which are endowed with the savor of enjoyment and remain forever steadfast.

O Lord, O Dhūrjaṭi, you who are skilled at destroying the suffering of those who bow before you, O treasure-house of auspiciousness; for me, who am terrified by birth and death and for whom [this world] is the sole abode of misery, act now so that, devoted solely to your worship, I may—while still living—attain the supreme, unshakable siddhis that grant the enjoyment of delightful sense-objects.
Homage to the one whose sole activity is the destruction of the great darkness of delusion,
who possesses the moon as his mark, and who is the light that excels all other forms of illumination.
The Twelfth Hymn, titled "The Revelation of the Secret":
No auxiliary cause is required for you, nor is any obstacle perceived; indeed, everything is already pervaded by you alone. Why, then, do you not see [it] even now? (UtSst 12.1)

May I always perceive [the Self] as free from all plurality, even though it appears to arise from the collection of entities, from the aggregate of the senses, from the midst of consciousness, or even as if originating from itself.
How could they be born, and how indeed could they come within the range of your vision? Yet, adorned with some naturally great mark,
you rise again and again and scatter from all things— land, water, grass, and so forth— the various objects of creation with floods of nectar flowing from that creation.
Satiated by the nectar flowing from the form of Your manifested presence, their thirst is uprooted; intoxicated with joy, they wander according to their pleasure.
Wherein there is no cognition of time—neither "not then," nor "always," nor even "at one time"—that is this system of yours; it is neither eternal, nor is it described otherwise.
May I always possess such perfection of yoga that my mind, longing for the sight of you, may enter your nectar-abode for the sake of worshipping you by mere intention alone. (UtS 12.6)
For those great-souled ones whose minds have blossomed through attaining your non-conceptual vision,
their stainless deeds and words shine forth clearly and effortlessly.
Dwelling right within the space between your two feet, free from fear,
may I worship you, O Lord, with unrestrained devotion throughout all those various realms of existence.
Completely merged within the interior of your lotus feet, with all other desires dissolved,
and thoroughly satiated by the excessive enjoyment of honey, may I wander according to my will.
Even for one whose resolve to worship you has arisen as if out of hypocrisy, your presence necessarily arises in a manner appropriate to them. (UtSst 12.10)

O Blessed One, with a mind that disregards all else and is entirely of one flavor, shall I drink to my heart's content from the Lord who lies within all things—something so easily obtained? (UtSst 12.11)
"All that is to be abandoned has been rejected by you, while that very [reality] which consists of you is to be accepted"— this is the summary of the essential point.

The multitude of entities that move within you are worshipped as being primarily identical with your own nature; how then could even those things outside of you, which are mere non-existence, be fit for the Lord or worthy of worship?
O Three-Eyed One, I shall behold You alone everywhere— silent, free from conceptual construction, undistracted, and beyond comparison— even amidst agitation, as one who is directly perceived.

O Lord, reveal Your own abode where You are eternally accompanied by the Supreme Goddess; for what reason would Your servants, who occupy a station equal to the dust of Your feet, appear as objects of distrust?
O Lord, even when you have come within the range of my sight, why do you withdraw from me, your servant?
For how long can you remain here, for not even a single moment, without being an object of the eyes of some living being?

O Lord, when—by means of the continuous, outpouring stream of the nectar of the consciousness of oneness—shall I attain supreme non-duality through immersion, and thus reach You and my own true nature in joy? (UtSst 12.17)
From this world of yours, which is secured by the realization that "I am," may even an atom's worth of that which rests upon the All be attained by me, so that I may be honored by you. (UtS 12.18)
Beholding that very same being in its immeasurable forms at every moment, may I clearly behold you alone, my own Lord, in your universal form.
Why does your mind not wander toward that very same desired object which has come into your presence?
For there is no injury to its nature; rather, it is only when my desire is fulfilled that yours is truly satisfied.
O Blessed One, by your power, it is said that hundreds of people— even those who act like common plowmen— behold your form ever before them with these very eyes.

That thought does not arise which is not composed of your will; whether it be auspicious or otherwise, it is ordained by the Blessed One in this way. Therefore, being of your very nature, as I wander or remain anywhere upon the earth, I am constantly engaged in the festival of worshipping your stainless feet, for that state is uncontradicted.
May eloquence properly arise before me regarding your profound utterances; and may my power to practice them likewise increase, as well as my unceasing devotion to worshiping you. (UtSst 12.23)
May this collection of objects always appear to me even in the context of conventional discourse,
just as it is a constituent part of your [teaching], and not because it has attained respectability in its own right.

May I always be skillful in serving you, such that even if my mind wanders here and there by its own force within the range of these [sensory] objects, it remains unperturbed even while engaged with them.
O Blessed One, it is solely by your will that I have become your servant; I possess no power of my own in this matter.
Yet, how is it that I behold your orb-like face? This is truly not a wonder.
For those who, filled with longing, gaze upon you whose form is so exceedingly beautiful—ah, what could have come to pass for them, or what means of attainment must have borne fruit? (UtS 12.27)
May all things exist as mere existence; may my becoming be through your becoming.
Thus, may there be nothing at all, nor anything other than you.
If it is nothing at all, let it remain nothing; yet let there be something, indeed something for me. In every way, may you thereby be one who has attained honor from all sides.

The Thirteenth Hymn, titled "The Compendium. O Lord, hear this summary concerning me: happiness and suffering are defined by my proximity to you and my separation from you, my Master. Union with you is happiness; separation from you, my Lord, is indeed suffering. (UtS 13.1)
O Lord, even that which is exceedingly subtle— the interval within me during which You were not manifest— please wipe away entirely and reveal Your own stainless true nature.

Whether my life remains or whether it has perished, let it be otherwise; may I always abide in Your body—which overflows with the universe, consists of the essence of the nectar of consciousness, and is beyond harm—constantly worshipping You, the Lord. (UtS 13.3)

"I am the lord, I alone am handsome, I am learned, I am fortunate; who else is my equal in the world?"—such pride is fitting for one who is devoted to you, but it is supreme [only] when directed toward you. (UtS 13.4)

O God of gods, by means of the knowledge of things as they truly are— which has arisen from your teaching of the non-dual nectar of reality and its subsequent withdrawal— make me worthy of worshipping your feet.
Thereafter, the Supreme Lord himself is meditated upon, then seen, and then touched;
may that great festival of worship be mine forever through your power.
Whether it be the vision of the reality established as it is, or that great festival of your worship—
this pair, being mutually dependent, always flourishes among those possessed of devotion.
May I remain intoxicated even while continuously drinking the elixir-liquor of the nectar of worshipping you through each of my senses, as all the goblets of my various states of being are filled.
O Lord, where not even an atom exists that is knowable by another, and where everything unfolds as self-luminous—
there, in Your city, grant a place for me, who am ever worshipping You.

O Supreme Lord, although I have been appointed to the station of a servant by Your own will, have I not been made a worthy recipient of Your very glance, or even of the task of massaging Your feet? (UtS 13.10)
O Lord, at the time of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), You never engage in deliberation;
what has come upon me today that You delay in the act of revealing Your own nature? (UtS 13.11)
In each and every object, both externally and internally, may I always behold you, the Supreme Goddess, who are united with [the Self], filling the three worlds, and being worshipped by my own hands.
Having ascended without hindrance at all times to the palace of the Lord by the mere power of my intention,
may I find the bliss obtained from the playful drinking of the supreme nectar-liquor of grace.
Because it bestows that wonder upon all auspicious objects through the mere act of touch, those possessed of unwavering devotion worship your body for that reason.
Pulsating with your own self, you expand the entire universe; touching the world, you touch its very form.
As you yourself whirl about with your own inner essence, that mandala of existence shines forth.
O Lord, for one who perceives this entire mandala of objects as non-conceptual and as Your very body,
and for whom the world is filled with their own self— how could there be any fear for such a person who is eternally blissful?
O Lord, even the Kālakūṭa poison resting in the hollow of Your throat is for me a great nectar;
yet even the nectar You have taken up [as Your own] does not please me if it remains distinct from Your body.
May I be adorned by speaking words that are consistent with reason, even while abandoning these songs of blood-red delirium;
and may my heart always be occupied by the beloved practice of worshipping you.
Alas, the will of the Supreme Lord cannot be calculated;
for even though he has granted me a body overflowing with nectar, he does not permit me to drink from it. (UtS 13.19)
O Lord of Umā, entering always into you— my own true nature, which is unfathomable, free from conceptual construction, non-dual, and the devourer of all objects— I would worship and offer praise.
The Fourteenth Hymn, titled "The Praise of Victory": Before my own Lord, the treasury of the goddess Jayalakṣmī,
may I for a moment savor the nectar-like essence of the proclamation of victory.
Victory to you, O Sole Rudra, O Sole Śiva, Mahādeva, Maheśvara;
O Śarva, beloved of Pārvatī, first-born of all the gods!

Victory to you, whose single eye is marked by the crescent moon, the sole ornament of the Lord of the Three Worlds! Victory to you, whose neck bears the dark Kālakūṭa poison as an ornament like a yellow garland of light!
Victory to you, whose form consists of the three powers, and whose hands shine with a hundred tridents;
victory to you, whose lotus feet are worthy of worship, for their purpose is accomplished by mere will.
Victory to you who possess a supramundane body overflowing with hundreds of beauties; victory to you who have taken on the ash from the Ganges as it flowed from your single matted lock!
Victory to you, who are anointed with the pale luster of moonlight spread across the Ocean of Milk;
victory to you, whose cold jewel-ornaments arise from the radiance of gems produced by contact with the body of Lord Śiva!
Victory to you, whose refuge is like a digit of the single, imperishable moon;
victory to you, who were consecrated in universal sovereignty by the ocean of the Gaṅgā!
Victory to you, who have purified Gokula by the touch of your lower limbs;
victory to you, who remain present for the assemblies of cowherds bound by devotion!
Victory to you, who deceive the foolish by the region of your own chosen splendor;
victory to you, the vessel of good fortune worthy of being embraced by Gaurī!

Victory to You, who are greedy for the offering of states of being ever-moist with the essence of devotional rasa; victory to You, who are delighted by the dancing words of devotees unrestrained in their devotion!
Victory to you, O Lord of the gods beginning with Brahmā, whose power is both manifest and inexhaustible! Victory to you, whose command is borne upon the heads of the entire host of world-protectors!
Victory to you, whose majesty is manifested by the self-seal placed upon the entire world;
victory to you, the Great Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, who culminates in the gift of your own self!
Victory to you, who have no second when desiring the creation of the three worlds; victory to you, whose only companion is the Goddess while bearing the weight of sovereign power!

Victory to you, who have completely traversed the three worlds with the sequence of your conquest; victory to you, whose sound as the Lord is sung by everyone from children upwards without exception! UtSst_14.14 //
Victory to you, who are naturally exalted regardless of qualities such as compassion;
victory to you, O Bhairava, who preceded the manifestation of the formidable Great Death!

Victory to you, whose fierce activity brings about the destruction of the universe and leaves no adversary; victory to you, the chanting of whose name is followed by hundreds of virtues and excellences!
Victory to you, O ocean that is the source of this nectar, bestowed with ease!
Victory to you, O fire whose momentary anger consumes the entire universe!
Victory to you, the sole lamp for the world of living beings blinded by the darkness of delusion! Victory to you, the Supreme Person who remains awake while the world sleeps!
Victory to you, O Jīvajīvaka warbling within the groves of the mountain of your body! Victory to you, O excellent Sārasa bird sporting in the sky of the noble mind!
Victory to you, Lord of Mountains, arisen from the supreme Jāmbūnada gold;
victory to you, the moon who brings about the calamity of falling meteors that revile the wicked!
Victory to you, difficult for even sages and gods to approach because of your arduous asceticism;
victory to you, who are gazed upon by the worlds as the wrestler who subdues the impurities of devotion in all ten directions!
Victory to you, who have made your own dependents recipients of the expansion of your own prosperity! Victory to you, whose sole purpose is the nurturing of those who have sought refuge in you!
Victory to you, the sole and pure cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
Victory to you, the festival for the bees that are the playful lotuses of the eyes of devoted women!

Victory, O vessel of victory! Victory, O conqueror of birth, old age, and death! Victory, O eldest in the world! Victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, O Three-Eyed One! (UtSst 14.24)
There are treatises named *Bhaktistotra* that wash away the three impurities;
those who have mastered them, as well as the yogis and scholars who are established in their own nature, are in truth your devotees alone. (UtSst 15.1)
O Lord, those who possess devotion and are nourished by the sustenance of illusory time, destiny, passion, and so forth, move about happily on the shore of the world.
Whether weeping or laughing, these devotees cry out to you loudly; their offerings consist solely of the utterance of words of praise. (UtSst 15.3)
May I not be one who is dispassionate nor even a lord seeking liberation while worshipping you;
rather, may I be intoxicated by the flavor of the wine of overflowing devotion.
O Lord, I bow to him who, having drawn the external [deity] within his very heart, worships you with floods of the nectar-essence of devotion.
Alas! Devoted to dharma and adharma, to action and knowledge, and likewise to pleasure and pain, these people experience some inexplicable inner state. (UtSst 15.6)

O Lord, even those who are blind and even those afflicted with leprosy shine most brilliantly when adorned with the intense ornament of devotion to You, the protector of all that moves and is stationary.
O Lord, even those whose limbs are withered by the heat of the sun and who subsist on gleaned grains, husks,
and roots, can subdue even the king of kings through the great heat of their devotion to you.
O Lord, some who stand all around you worship you with their very minds alone— minds that, though still desiring to ascend, are rolling even as they are moistened by devotion to you.
O Lord, this great wealth of devotion to you— which removes the miseries of saṃsāra— must be protected, increased, and held in high esteem.
O Lord, although your devotees are full of passion for you,
nevertheless, may their mistress always be satisfied with them, having abandoned all jealousy.
When devotion to you arises, the state of worldly existence that was previously imminent is destroyed; once the great jar of milk has been obtained, one’s greed for curds is abandoned.
Is this not incomparable accomplishment? Or does it not flow with the foremost happiness—that devotion which becomes eternally established toward Śambhu as it is cultivated? (UtS 15.13)
Alas, while my mind is defiled, the jewel-creeper of devotion to you has sunk within it;
it does not even produce its own non-human splendors arising from its innate excellence. (UtSst 15.14)
Devotion toward the Blessed One, the Lord of the three worlds, indeed becomes the supreme accomplishment;
yet, because it is devoid of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, that very devotion is not complete—this is my reflection. (UtSst 15.15)
Exuding an intense fragrance from clusters of *utpala* flowers both externally and internally,
these auspicious [perfumes] permeate all the yogis living nearby, even those whose mental dispositions are contrary.

There is not even a trace of light by word; the entire universe is in a state of profound, total sleep, yet on this occasion of Śivarātri, O Lord, the devotees constantly worship you therein. (UtSst 15.17)
May my being expand within the auspicious Lord, whose qualities are truth; may the masses of dust rising from the feet of Śaṅkara shine upon the crest during worship;

may even the latent impressions of memory regarding passion and the like be utterly destroyed; O Śambhu, may darkness prevail for me in the dissolution of myself into You, or else may the triad of the gunas prevail.

The path of saṃsāra is very long; my body-staff has been scorched by various most cruel diseases. Though I have never enjoyed pleasures, nor have I ever experienced happiness for long, I have thus become one whose life is in vain—yet my head is beautiful, being trodden upon by Your feet that bear the moon. Since I am Your devotee, grant me immediately, O Possessor of Great Wealth, exceedingly long-lasting riches.
The sixteenth hymn, named "The Severing of the Noose."
There is nothing whatsoever that constitutes an obscuration to you for the worlds;
there is nothing whatsoever that constitutes an obscuration to you for your devotees.
Even though You are reached through the stages of skillful means and are complex with manifold attributes, Your self appears once and for all as pure to those who possess devotion.
"O Lord, even those who are victorious laugh, and even those who are defeated laugh;
for only a few are so intoxicated by drinking the nectar of devotion to you."
May I never attain success, nor may I ever be liberated;
rather, may I be filled with the nectar of devotion, having reached the supreme pinnacle of the most delicious [flavor].
O Lord, just as this essence of devotion to you was previously unknown to me, may that very same [devotion] now be fully nourished once it has been established.
By this truth, O Blessed One, may there be no further scope for my prayers;
may I simply possess that same kind of intense immersion in devotion toward him forever.
Though intoxicated by devotion, I might still become angry and harbor latent tendencies toward worldly existence; likewise, I might laugh, cry out, or even shout "Śiva! excessively. (UtS 16.7)
O Lord, through devotion, may I be so even when situated in adversity, even when in health, even when weeping, even when laughing, even when profound, and even when distracted.
For devotees, there is nothing to be perceived within you or outside of you,
where you yourself abide as the non-conceptual one whose nature is pure consciousness.
Even when you are being reviled, your devotees rejoice within as if pierced by drops of nectar, struck by the sharp needles of horripilation.
Even painful sensation serves as enjoyment for those who possess devotion,
for whose every consciousness is moistened by nectar and consists of the moonlight of you.
For devotees who are confined here and there, whether outside or inside,
the bliss of tasting the flavor of the touch of your body is equal and free from artifice.
Some, having eliminated the element of wretchedness inherent in the dualistic refuge of ritual worship toward You, O Lord, relish Your pure body composed of nectar.
The views of the non-Buddhists are deluded and divided, for their very divisions arise from delusion; yet you alone shine as the one, peerless reality for your devotees.

How could one whose mind is stainless due to the ripening of the cessation of pride, contempt, passion, and so forth, be a person of devotion who possesses conduct equal to that of worldly people? (UtS 16.15)

In the presence of those great beings by whom even the darkness of passion and hatred has been conquered by the light of devotion, who among those possessed of mere intellectual knowledge could stand before them?
For one who possesses the means for the practice of bathing in and drinking the nectar of devotion, there is a state of sublime ease throughout the stages of its commencement, middle, and conclusion.
Fame is to be sought as an object of thought, and you alone are to be honored;
therefore, for those possessing devotion to you, the course of worldly life becomes praiseworthy as it consists of you.
O Lord, it is only through devotion toward you that the notion of liberation has ripened;
having ascended to its first stage, we are therefore as if already liberated.
"O Lord, for one whose soul is filled with devotion to you, even a great onset of suffering is acceptable;
may a succession of pleasures never be directed away from you."
"You are pleased by devotion, and when You are pleased, O Lord, there is devotion; since these two are mutually dependent, it is as You Yourself know how that is appropriate."
O Lord, whether with form or formless, whether within or without, you are in every way composed of nectar for those who possess devotion.
Within this very world, for one who possesses devotion toward you, there exists another fruit altogether, which is the manifestation of joy. (UtS 16.23)

Devotion to the secret, devotion to the supreme, devotion to the Great Lord of the universe—to you, Śambhu, the auspicious God; oh, what an indescribable thing indeed is called "devotion"! UtSst_16.24.
Devotion, devotion to the Supreme; devotion is indeed most intense—I utter this cry so that there may be fervent devotion for you, the Supreme. (UtSst 16.25)
Since I am, O Lord, a source for all beauties,
whatever is attached to you would be priceless, whether it be a jewel or even a blade of grass.
Victorious are those who dwell in existence, for whom there is no separation from You on the path of pure awareness, extending from the knower down to the object known.
O Lord, you are embraced by some outside the theater of saṃsāra, while others, right there within it, embrace you with their fetters cast off and their weariness gone. (UtS 16.28)
I bow to Śiva, who is firmly embraced by Śivā— who has enjoyed all the world as her food, drink, and adornment— and who is impetuous with the joy of the festival of universal dissolution.

Victorious is Your unprecedented supreme lordship, O Lord of the Universe, which is devoid of anything to be ruled; and likewise victorious is Your other [lordship] by which this world appears, yet does not appear as it truly is.
The seventeenth hymn, titled "Great Regard for Divine Play":
Ah! Victorious is this wondrous, sweet, and great festival of worship, for it causes even the tears to yield fully the taste of the essence of nectar. (UtSst_17.1)
All activities preceded by your worship grant success; for all those devoted to you, being identical with you, they are themselves the very perfections.
Those who incessantly worship you— who exist at all times and in all things, simultaneously possessing every form— they are my presiding deities.
May that festival of touching you, accomplished through the non-disregard of meditative concentration and renowned as the ritual of worship, always be mine, O Devotion! (UtSst 17.4)
For devotees, the equinox of the essence of equanimity is ever-present;
their constant worship consists of the nectar-essence of the flavor of your being.
O Lord, for that ritual which has no beginning or end and no sequence of time,
its performer is one who is devoted to You, the Supreme.
Even Brahmā and the other gods are masters and partakers of good fortune for those in whose dreams, or even in their delusion, there remains the festival of your worship.
For those who recite prayers, offer oblations, bathe, and meditate—not only these, but for devotees whenever and wherever they perform worship unto you—[there is no suffering]. (UtSst 17.8)

Who indeed is equal to those who are always happy through the enjoyment of tasting the nectar of your worship—be they Indra and the other gods, or even the foremost among them, such as Brahmā? (Udānavarga 17.9)
In this great festival of worship of yours, which alone causes the agitation of the world,
whatever may be attained is known only by the devotees.

Abiding in Your abode, which consists of pure consciousness, I shall always worship You, O All-pervading Lord, through the activities of the thirty-six principles and through the movements of body, speech, and mind.
May all my time pass away—whether it be brief or even infinite—for me who finds joy in the bliss of enjoyment through unattached devotion to you; this is what I pray for.
O Lord, may my greed for the enjoyment of the nectar-flavor of your worship increase day by day and always bear fruit.
May I always remain worshipping you, the Great-Souled One, in your ocean which is filled with the singular flavor of nectar born from the dissolution of the world.
In the ritual of worship, your devotees always offer their mind— made straight by the severing of the knots of all latent tendencies— as a sweet oblation unto you.
Having presided over these objects, the functions of the senses send forth the nectar-liquor for the sake of Your worship by Your devotees. (UtSst 17.16)
For those devotees whose minds are rendered helpless by the great heat of the intensity of their devotion,
what other cause for nirvāṇa could there be than immersion in the nectar of your worship?
O Lord, may the great festival of drinking the nectar of constantly worshipping Your feet be the sole cause for my attainment of Your grace.
O Lord, having experienced at every moment the great bliss of tasting the nectar of drinking your worship, which is the fruit of every action, from moment to moment; UtSst_17.19 //
For devotees, the great effort of worshiping you has its purpose realized right here and now, since they experience at that very moment a happiness that was previously inconceivable. (UtS 17.20)
As long as one has not obtained the great festival of tasting the nectar of worshiping you,
I believe that not even a fraction of the abundance of happiness has been tasted.
For devotees, without even the exertion of the semblance of searching for sense objects, that state of abiding in your abode arises effortlessly during their acts of worship. (UtSst 17.22)
There is nothing unattainable for devotees, nor is there anything difficult for them to obtain;
they wander about solely intoxicated by the pride of worshipping you.
O Giver of Boons, how wonderful is this unique method of worship for those whose minds are noble with the weight of devotion toward you— a method that is not stained by the taint of begging!
What beauty is there that is not [found here], what joy, what prosperity, or what else? What liberation is there that is not attained when this Great God (Mahādeva) is worshipped?
May this body of mine, nourished by the nectar of pure and transparent devotion shining from within, be for the purpose of worshiping you.
O All-pervading Lord, may I always be dependent upon the enjoyment of worshipping Your feet;
O Sovereign of the worlds, may I be the sole one who acts according to my own will.
O Lord, for those who thirst for meditation upon you, for the sight of you, and for the touch of you,
there arises the great lake of your worship— cool and sweet.
Just as you alone are the vessel for the world’s offerings and enjoyments,
O Lord, so too is only the devoted one the vessel for offerings and enjoyments.
O Lord, may this great festival of your worship be victorious,
wherein the agitation of even the thirty-six principles exults intensely.
Homage to them, O All-pervading Lord, for whom even the implements used for Your worship become objects of worship themselves through the nectar-water of their devotion.

O Lord, at the commencement of worship, having meditated upon the identity with You that is to be infused by the mantra, the devotees, being absorbed in the Supreme within their own selves, do not find room anywhere else for their joy. (UtSst 17.32)
In the great festival of worship, some, blooming as if at the attainment of a kingdom,
share the entire world with the nectar of ambrosia.
Those whose enjoyment at every moment consists of worship and the drinking of the nectar of immortality— are they gods, or are they liberated ones, or are they some other kind of people?
Through assuming every form as an instrument of worship, he displays a certain profound respect for his devotees, and yet a certain measure of lightness. (UtS 17.35)
From the agitation caused by the distraction of the senses during worship, nectar emerges for the devotees,
just as it does for the gods from the churning of the ocean of milk.
Some consider worship to be like a wish-fulfilling cow;
others, with their faces turned inward, suckle upon its essence, which is sweeter than a stream of nectar.
Even this flickering of the eyes among devotees is considered [by the Lord] as worldly existence;
having drawn them inward, it nourishes a great festival of worship within. (UtS 17.38)

O Lord, when worship is performed toward You, who are one's own self, through the power of the agitation of devotion, it is not strange that this does not lead to wretchedness; rather, it is the supreme fruit of humility.
For some devotees, ritual service is a means for attaining Your state; however, for them, it is rather an expansion of the bliss arising from their identity with You. (UtSst 17.40)

Even when expanded by those unrestrained by the intoxication of devotion to the worship of forms that are essentially unconnected [to you], it attains an indescribable stability within you. (UtS 17.41)
O Śambhu, you alone are indeed the graceful recipient of offerings, for your mind has become fixed upon the tasting of the flavor of delicious food, even as it falls away.
O Lord, may my means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the ritual of worshiping you be complete, pure, full of devotion, and steadfast. (UtSst 17.43)
O Lord, in this ritual of worshipping you— a treasury of every kind of offering— oh,
some indescribable splendor unfolds within the multitude of my senses!
O Protector, this very gentleness of yours alone is indeed perceived,
in that even the Lord of the Universe is worshipped by your servants and is attained through them.
Whether from a conditioned or unconditioned entity, or even from non-existence,
may the great festival of worship for you arise for me, who am already praiseworthy.
I am truly pleased with those who always worship you through desire, anger, and pride—even when these have been offered up; salutations to them! (UtS 17.47)
Victorious is this supreme rite of worship for those who partake in devotion to you,
which, even when performed with blades of grass, is as effective as if it were fashioned with jewels.
The Eighteenth Hymn:
Manifestation Having found You within the world, they again find this [world] within You;
O Lord of the World, for those who partake in devotion to You alone, there is nothing here that remains beyond their reach. (UtS 18.1)
In some places you are Bhava, and in some places Bhavānī, the preeminent one who contains within her the sequence of all purposes;
yet in the state of ultimate reality, there is no distinction between you and the Goddess, nor even between the three worlds.
Arrogant people do not recognize even that which is beautiful, for all things are indeed made beautiful through effort;
yet this mind, though striving, does not perceive its own true nature here—alas, oh, I am ruined!
I bow to him who, having worshipped your feet with the abundance of wealth obtained by dwelling within his own self which consists of existence,
does not even constantly require food or clothing.
Although this world always dwells securely within your body, it burns intensely within;
therefore, by your will, act so that I may become filled with the bliss of worshipping you here.
May my mind be intent on drinking the nectar of worshiping the pair of your lotus feet, which arise spontaneously;
and may I conduct my life’s journey with only the touch of happiness regarding the accumulation of all that is beneficial.
O Lord, within You who clearly manifest as the sphere of all worldly activity,
may my objects— constantly appearing and disappearing— shine forth at all times.
I would always wander with you in your very city, never separated from you;
let not even a moment or a fraction of a second pass for me without victory, wherein you are present.
Filled on all sides by the floods of cool nectar flowing from your limbs, the devotees here, through the excellence of worshipping you, move within the lake of saṃsāra.
O Lord, may I always dwell within my own self in your great forest, which is cooled by the shade of the great tree of mantras, as your worshiper.

O Lord, just as you appear before me as the embodiment of creative intuition (pratibhā), manifesting from every object and from all living beings, so too may you come forth before me, adorned with the splendor of the three eyes and the trident.
When will you, having attained satisfaction through the offering of my own conceit and through the weight of devotion conceived as "mine-ness," become the object of my vision everywhere?
Dwelling in the midst of the ocean of supreme nectar, with my mind immersed solely in the ritual of worshipping you,
may I perform every human activity while experiencing some small measure of that essence everywhere.
Let your own substance remain here; who indeed is fit to explain the reality of this matter?
For it is this very thing—name, form, activity, and so forth—that seizes you away, since you are Hara.

They had not the slightest desire for pleasure for the sake of peace; nor did they offer before the Lord—a heart-stealer—any prayer for the fruit of seeking liberation, since their pride was nourished by devotion. (UtS 18.15)
Whether it be the state of wakefulness, the other state of sleep, or any other slight condition whatsoever,
for those people who are vessels of devotion and whose minds are protected by You, all of that is a great festival.

O Lord, how can the fluctuations of my own senses— which are everywhere of a lax nature— remain so once they have attained You, who possess firm and far-reaching consciousness and are warmed by the wealth of devotion?

Nothing distinct was ever created, nor was anything here fashioned that is other than happiness; yet you are in every way the abode of wonder, being both subject to suffering and distinct—homage be to you!

May I behold you constantly— my impurities of conceptual construction washed away by the overflowing nectar of the sword that negates harshness, and the enemy of doubt, so difficult to conquer, shattered.
Therefore, O Lord, enter me clearly so that I may always enter you;
for by this means, having attained supreme proximity, I may worship your very form directly with fervor.
No one possesses the power to praise you, or rather, they do indeed possess it because you are so exceedingly beautiful; yet this is my constant prayer: that I might behold the Lord without ceasing.

Victorious is Śiva, the true wish-fulfilling tree, whose history is unprecedented, who bestows diverse fruits upon those who have transcended the stage of mere petition, and who is celebrated by the name Udyotana; this is the nineteenth hymn.
Since everything is indeed obtainable by you from your own self alone, as it is the sole repository of all things;
yet for me, that very self of mine is not you, who are the supreme [reality] beyond that.
The Self, whose body consists of consciousness, action, and knowledge, is in every respect the Supreme Lord himself;
for what else could there not be, indeed, among all these various objects, but his very form? (UtSst 19.3)

O Lord, by means of this fruit which steals away the pain of suffering— your very self in the form of my vision— may I, having merged with it, attain a state of being identical with you through that path.

O Blessed One, when will that perfection be achieved for me— perfection adorned by the wish-fulfilling gem creeper of meditating upon your stainless feet, and which produces wonder in the minds of the perfected ones?
O Lord, when shall I behold your stainless countenance,
from which flows a flood of unprecedented nectar that submerges the entire universe without exception?

O Lord, when will your form, which is joyful merely by being meditated upon, forever fill the vast chasms of my ignorance regarding the liberation known as non-difference from you with floods of supreme nectar? (UtSst 19.7)
O Lord, my mind has not yet abandoned its fickleness due to attachment to the unsurpassed flavor of your [teachings]; when will this come to pass quickly? (UtSst 19.8)
May I not always obtain from others only things that are dry and bitter; rather, may all kinds of dualities, even those involving suffering, fall upon me.
O Lord, may your pure rays come face to face with me, so that [I] may be cleansed of the darkness of the afflictions of body and mind.
O Lord, be gracious until those who obstruct my path to you—
those thieves of virtue who steal away the ultimate truth— are brought under control.
O Lord, may my mind be quickly filled with the showers of the nectar of devotion to you,
so that these worthless latent tendencies may be swept away entirely by plunging into it.
If devotion to you does not shine even in one who possesses the nature of a mortal during the state of liberation, then why should it?
O Unborn One, therefore lead me to the corresponding stage of perfection.
O Lord, do not treat me with contempt because I am greedy for even a fraction of supernatural powers;
for liberation shines forth from the side of the *aṇimā* and other powers only when one is emaciated by devotion to You.
May the Blessed One be gracious to me, his slave; indeed, this much alone I beg:
that the Giver, the Lord of the Three Worlds, should not be beyond the range of the eyes of those such as I.
May the pair of your lotus feet always blossom within my mind— which is filled with the nectar-essence of the remembrance of your form— and distill some indescribable, world-transcending honey.
"I have that Lord Janaka as my master, or else Tryambaka; and Bhavānī is my mother.
There is no second person here who belongs to me. Thinking thus, I would wander about most contented.

I praise the Lord, the Master of the three worlds, who is white with ashes, three-eyed, and bearer of the trident; he who has a serpent as his sacred thread, whose crest is the digit of the moon, and who is known by the name Carvaṇa— this twentieth hymn.
I bow to him whose white lower garment is the halo formed by the silken cloth slipping from his own body,
and who has fashioned a festive adornment for his dance with a shimmering garland of skulls.
I bow to those deities whose very gestures are worthy of Hara,
whose lives are ever devoted solely to Hara, and who are the eternal abodes of good fortune.
This very play of your sovereignty is something else entirely;
for in these avadānas, which are accomplished by mere wish, I myself employ the supreme means.
O Lord, when such play occurs within this world of yours, which is worthy of universal veneration,
how great must be the resulting surge of the essence of bliss!
How could he not be fortunate who is Hara, the beloved of Gaurī?
And how could even Hara not be so, since he is the supreme beloved of Gaurī?
The consciousness-creepers of that certain great tree are of such a nature, having as their root his own self which consists of the nectar of meditative absorption and is imperishable.
O Supreme Lord, at the moment of the outburst of the itching of devotion,
worship alone arises as the great pillar of the touchstone.
Salutations to the Lord, who always finds delight in creation, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance, and who is ever satisfied by devouring the three worlds.
Homage again and again to those fortunate ones who, having gone nowhere and abandoned nothing at all, behold this very world as your own abode.
For those enriched by the fortune of devotion, what else remains to be prayed for?
And for those impoverished of it, what else remains to be prayed for?
Where suffering becomes happiness, even poison becomes nectar,
and cyclic existence becomes liberation— that is the path of Śaṅkara.
O Lord, for those who enjoy worldly existence, there is no suffering in the beginning, the middle, or the end;
nevertheless, we are sinking—how can this be explained?
O Lord, just as light is available to those who act according to their own will, you ought to regard even others through the yoga of knowledge and other means, for they possess devotion.
For your devotees, there are no afflictions, nor is there any anxiety regarding their own selves;
nevertheless, this something indescribable known as "Śiva" exists within them, even as they remain outwardly directed.
O Lord, I praise that power of action of Yours, which, permeated by the force of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), illumines all appearances as "I am this. (UtS 20.16)
All living beings without exception—even Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu—exist as they are swallowed by you; therefore, O Lord, I praise the universe which consists of your being.
"O Protector, because all things are connected to destruction, everything other than me is false; thus it is proclaimed by you in the play of withdrawal. (UtS 20.18)
O Giver of Boons, for those whose wealth is devotion, your form stands present before them as soon as it is meditated upon;
and your victories prevail in bringing about all wonders, even regarding that which is inconceivable.
As if sprinkled with the nectar of the flavor of devotion to you, the circle of his vital organs throbbing with bliss,
the heroic man dances at night, emboldened by throngs of *vetāla* spirits.
O Śambhu, may that very limb of mine by which this hymn of praise to you was begun remain firm and entirely unimpaired throughout this entire, boundless time.
